#### Three window shapes through one assigner

**What is being answered.** Why there are three window shapes — as one `assign` function that can answer for two of them and must return NONE for the third.

`assign(e, shape)` returns a **list**: one element for fixed, up to 2 for sliding, and NONE for a session. `totalAcross` then multiplies `e.v` by that list's length, which is the whole mechanism behind the sliding total exceeding the dataset.

Step 2 is the structural point: a session cannot be assigned from a single event, because its bounds depend on events that have not arrived. Step 4 shows the consequence — `gap` is the only difference between 3 sessions and 4.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-shapes-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: fixed and sliding differ only in the LENGTH of the answer" width="980">

For id 4, `assign` returns [240] under "fixed" and [180, 240] under "sliding" — a list of 2. `totalAcross` multiplies `e.v` by `len(...)`, which is why the sliding total reaches 78 against 45. The overlap is in the list length, nowhere else.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — a session cannot be assigned from one event at all</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-shapes-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: a session cannot be assigned from one event at all" width="980">

The fall-through returns NONE for "session" — not an oversight. A session's bounds depend on events that have not arrived, so no function of a single event can name them. That is the structural reason sessions need the separate `sessionize` pass, and the reason they can be revised later.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — so sessions are built by comparing CONSECUTIVE event times</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-shapes-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: so sessions are built by comparing CONSECUTIVE event times" width="980">

The event at et 130 is compared against `last.end` = 3: the difference is 127, which exceeds GAP = 120, so the `if` fails and the next line starts a new session. One subtraction and one comparison decide every session boundary in the book.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and the same events give a different number of sessions</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch04-shapes-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and the same events give a different number of sessions" width="980">

`wide` holds 3 sessions and `tight` holds 4, from identical events — only `gap` differed. Both heap rows are correct answers to "how many visits did key a have?", which means the question is not answerable until the gap is stated. It is a definition, not a tuning parameter.

</details>
